sections.title: Masses and Springs · Theory and Prediction
One mass, two directions

teaching.text: A **mass-spring system** is a mass hooked up to a spring, and it vibrates because of what each part wants. **The spring wants to be at its equilibrium position**, its resting length, so whenever it is stretched or squished it pulls or pushes to get back there. **A mass that is moving wants to keep on moving**, so once it gets going it does not stop on its own.
children: When the mass is pulled out and let go, the spring pulls it back toward equilibrium.
The mass is still moving when it gets there, so it keeps on moving past equilibrium and squishes the spring, which then pushes it back the other way.
The mass overshoots again and again, so the system vibrates. Friction from the table would slowly stop it, but the model leaves friction out, so in the model it vibrates forever.

teaching.text: The same system can be pictured in **two directions**, and it is important to be able to picture it both ways. In the **longitudinal** picture the mass moves left and right along the line of the spring, and in the **transverse** picture the mass sits between two walls with a spring on each side and goes up and down.
children: Pulling the mass up in the transverse picture stretches the springs, and because springs hate being extended, they pull the mass back down.
When the mass passes the middle, the springs are not stretched at all, but the mass is moving, so it keeps on moving and stretches them on the other side.

teaching.text: **Both pictures move in exactly the same way** and at the same rate, because they have the same mass and the same total stiffness. Some systems are easier to think about longitudinally and others transversely, but both describe the same vibration.
children: So the rate of vibration is set by the mass and the stiffness, not by which direction the mass happens to move.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate

teaching.text: Two things set how fast a mass-spring system vibrates, and they are the **mass** and the **stiffness** of the spring. The number of back-and-forth cycles the system completes each second is called its **frequency**.
children: Each comparison changes only one of these two things, so its effect is easy to see.

teaching.text: **A heavier mass vibrates more slowly**, and this matches everyday experience, since heavy branches sway back and forth slowly while little branches sway back and forth quickly. A heavy mass is hard to get moving and hard to turn around, so each trip back and forth takes longer.
children: So making the mass much heavier, while the spring stays the same, makes the whole system vibrate at a noticeably lower rate.

teaching.text: **A stiffer spring makes the system vibrate faster.** Stiffness is harder to picture than mass, but the idea is that the stiffer something is, the faster it wants to go back, because a stiff spring pulls back hard and turns the mass around sooner.
children: So making the spring much stiffer, while the mass stays the same, makes the whole system vibrate at a noticeably higher rate.
Both rules hold whether the system is pictured longitudinally or transversely.

teaching.text: The two rules point in **opposite directions**, because raising the mass lowers the frequency while raising the stiffness raises the frequency.
children: These two rules are what explain everything about modes, strings and, eventually, speech.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes

teaching.text: With **two masses**, the system has two walls, a spring from each wall to a mass, and one spring between the two masses. All the masses are equal and all the springs are equal, and this system can vibrate in **two different ways**, which are called **modes**. **A mode is just another word for a way of vibrating**, and the two modes are told apart by asking whether the masses go together or against each other.
children: In the first mode, both masses are pulled up and let go, and they go up and down together, or in the longitudinal picture they move left and right together.
In the second mode, one mass is pulled down and the other up, and they move against each other, so whenever one goes up the other goes down.

teaching.text: A system can also vibrate in **both modes at the same time**. If both masses are pulled up but one higher than the other, both start falling together, which is the first mode, while the middle spring also pushes them against each other, which is the second mode.
children: The result moves together and against each other at once, and real systems, including the ones used in speech production, do this all the time.

teaching.text: **The second mode vibrates faster than the first**, even though both use the same two masses and the same three springs. The explanation comes from asking what each spring is actually doing in each mode.
children: In the first mode the masses move together, so the middle spring never stretches or compresses. It just rides along like a rigid bar, so effectively the first mode has only two springs.
In the second mode the masses move against each other, so the middle spring is stretched and squished over and over, and all three springs are working.

More springs working means more stiffness, and more stiffness means more pull and so a higher frequency. Nothing about the springs themselves changed, because the two modes simply use the springs differently.

teaching.text: This foundation has to be followed step by step rather than memorized, because each later idea builds on it.
children: The general rule is that the more the masses go against each other, the more the springs stretch and compress, so the higher the frequency of that mode.

sections.title: Pop quiz
Three masses have three normal modes

teaching.text: With **three masses**, the system has **three modes**, one more than with two masses, and each mode is a different way the masses move relative to each other. In the first mode all three go back and forth together, and this mode has the lowest frequency. In the second mode the middle mass stays perfectly still while the two outer masses move against each other, and this is the middle frequency. In the third mode the middle mass moves opposite to the two outer masses, and this is the highest frequency.
children: The second mode can be started by carefully leaving the middle mass untouched and pulling the two outer masses apart.
The third mode is easiest to see in the transverse picture, with the middle going one way while the sides go the other.

teaching.text: The frequencies follow the same reasoning as with two masses. The first mode is very slow because the masses move together, so the two middle springs are doing nothing, and since their job is to stretch and compress, which is what raises frequency, they add no stiffness when they just ride along.
children: In the second mode the springs do stretch and compress, but not as much as they could.
In the third mode everything is going against everything else, so there is lots of stretching and lots of compression, which uses the most stiffness and makes it the fastest.
The masses and springs are identical in all three modes, so only the way the masses move relative to each other changes the frequency.

teaching.text: All three modes can also happen **at the same time**, and however the system is started, it vibrates as some mix of its pure modes.
children: Learning an instrument means learning how to excite some modes and not others, and those favored modes are heard as notes.
With four masses the same logic continues, giving four modes that range from all the masses moving together to every mass moving against its neighbors.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: The pattern holds for any number of masses, since **N masses give N modes**. One mass has only one way to vibrate, two masses have two ways, three have three, and so on. Moving to higher modes, more parts move against each other, so there are more reversals in the pattern and the frequency gets higher.
children: In chains of separate masses like these, the mode frequencies are generally not whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency.

teaching.text: Comparing the same mode across chains of different lengths reveals the same idea repeating. Every first mode has all the masses going up and down together, every second mode has the left side going against the right side, and every third mode has the middle going against the sides.
children: When the number of masses is odd, the middle mass in the second mode is frozen while the sides go against each other around it.

teaching.text: Packing in more and more masses and springs, all the way to an infinite number, gives a **string**, like a guitar or piano string. Every little piece of a string has mass, and every little piece stretches like a spring, so a string vibrates in exactly the same kinds of modes.
children: In the lowest mode the whole string goes up and down together with hardly any stretching between its pieces, and that mode gives the lowest note.
In higher modes more and more parts of the string move against each other, and a string plucked without any skill vibrates in many modes at once.

teaching.text: A system can also be **fixed on one side and free to sway on the other**, and a **building** is like this, because it is fixed to the ground at the bottom and free to sway at the top in high winds or earthquakes.
children: Civil engineers design buildings to sway in the first mode, all together, and never in higher modes, where some floors would move one way while others move the other way.
Buildings are not made so stiff that they cannot move at all, because they are designed to sway safely in their lowest mode.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: A **string fixed at both ends** vibrates in many modes. In the lowest mode the whole string goes up and down together, and each higher mode has more sections moving against each other and completes more cycles in the same amount of time. Frequency is measured in **Hertz**, which means times per second.
children: For a string fixed at both ends, each mode is a **whole-number multiple** of the lowest one, so the second mode is twice the lowest, the third is three times the lowest, and so on. Modes that line up this way are called **consecutive harmonics**.
The motion is slowed way down so that it can be followed by eye.

teaching.text: A real string vibrates in **all of its modes at the same time**, so its actual motion is the sum of all of them. Adding the separate motions together at every point gives one complicated, changing shape, which is what an actual plucked string does.
The **spectrum** of a sound tells which frequencies are in it and how much of each there is.
children: For a string moving in five modes at once, the spectrum has five spikes, one at the frequency of each moving mode.

If the string vibrated only in its third mode, there would be no movement in the other modes, so the spectrum would have just one spike, at the frequency of the third mode. That pattern is like a one-hot encoding, with one active slot and every other slot at zero.
So the spectrum turns a complicated motion into a simple list of which modes are moving and how strongly.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: **The vocal folds are even more complicated than strings.** They are a bunch of muscle forming a surface, which is called a **membrane**, and a membrane spreads its masses and springs across two directions instead of along one line. The same logic of modes still applies to them.
children: In the first mode all the masses go up and down together, and in the second mode the left half goes against the right half.
In the third mode the middle is stuck while the sides go against each other, and higher modes divide the surface into more and more parts.

teaching.text: The frequencies given to the membrane's modes in the picture are assigned for teaching, so they are not the natural frequencies this particular rectangle would really have.
children: Adding all of the motions together gives one combined surface, and measured at one point, its spectrum has equal spikes, one for each mode.

teaching.text: In real vocal folds, **all the modes happen at the same time**. Producing a voice makes the vocal folds vibrate in many modes at once, and that is what creates a spectrum full of spikes.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction

teaching.text: **The scientific method depends on very clear statements about how systems work.** These statements are usually written as **differential equations**, which describe how quantities change over time, and solving the equations gives a prediction about how the world will behave when it is actually measured.
children: The simple spring equation is one example, because solving it predicts that a pulled spring goes back and a pushed spring also goes back.

teaching.text: For the voice, the theory says that **the vocal folds are a membrane** built from many masses and springs, so they vibrate in many modes at once. Their equations are the same type as the spring equations, only more of them and slightly more complicated, so the intuition built from masses and springs is enough to reason with. The prediction is that **any laryngeal vibration signal will have a spectrum with evenly spaced spikes**, and these evenly spaced spikes are called **harmonics**.

**This prediction was tested in class.** Two students each made a sound with the mouth wide open, so that no particular vowel was being made, and the spectrum of each voice was examined in the program Praat.
children: In the first student's voice the spikes came at a low frequency and its multiples, evenly spaced just as predicted.
In the second student's voice the first spike was about twice as high, and the following spikes were again evenly spaced, only farther apart.
So the prediction held for both voices, and a prediction built from intuition about masses and springs turned out to be precise and real.

teaching.text: The difference between the two voices follows from the mass rule. The second voice has a higher pitch, so that student's vocal folds are probably smaller and thinner, and thinner folds have less mass, so they vibrate at a higher frequency.
children: This is part of how people are recognized by their voices, since becoming familiar with someone means becoming familiar with the spectrum of their voice.
How a person says particular vowels also matters, and that depends on the air above the vocal folds rather than the folds themselves.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: A string can also be **fixed at one end and free at the other**, like a building that is fixed to the ground and sways at the top. At the fixed bottom the string cannot move, and a point that never moves is called a **node**. At the free top the string moves the most, and a point of largest motion is called an **antinode**.
children: So every mode has to start with a node at the bottom and end with an antinode at the top.

teaching.text: This changes which modes are possible, because **only the odd harmonics occur**, meaning one, three, five and seven times the lowest frequency. The modes at two and four times the lowest frequency are missing, because those patterns cannot end with free motion at the top.
children: The first mode has no still point inside the string, and its motion grows steadily from the fixed bottom to the free top, like a building swaying as a whole.
Each higher mode adds more still points inside, with more sections swinging against each other.

teaching.text: Freeing one end also lowers the whole system. For a string of the same length and wave speed, switching from fixed at both ends to fixed at one end and free at the other **halves the lowest frequency**.
children: When both ends are fixed, the string has every whole-number multiple of the lowest frequency.
When one end is fixed and the other is free, the string has only the odd multiples.

lecture12.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production

sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Dynamic systems in economic stabilization

teaching.text: This year's **Nobel Prize in economics** went to work on **stabilization**, which means getting a system to equilibrium and keeping it there. That is the same **balancing feedback** a spring has, since a spring that is pulled or pushed always goes back to equilibrium.
children: The prize was described as work on **boom-bust cycles**, the economy's repeated swings between good times and bad times.

teaching.text: In that picture, **unemployment and inflation go in reverse of each other**, rising and falling like the two oscillating curves of a mass-spring system. One curve behaves like **x**, the position of the mass, and the other behaves like its flip, **v**, the velocity.
children: So the same math that describes masses and springs also describes the economy, just in a completely different domain.

teaching.text: The winning theory is called **Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium**. The word **dynamic** says it describes how the economy changes over time, the word **stochastic** says it allows for unpredictable shocks, and the words **general equilibrium** say the goal is an economy that settles into balance.
children: Stabilization policy tries to damp the swings so that the oscillations get smaller and smaller, much as SGD comes back to the average after one wildly off number.

sections.title: One mass, two directions

teaching.text: A mass-spring system rests on two facts, which are that **the spring wants to be at its equilibrium position** and that **a moving mass keeps on moving**. When the mass is pulled and let go, the spring pulls it back, the mass overshoots because it keeps moving, and so the system vibrates.
children: The model leaves out gravity and friction and only cares about the springs pulling toward equilibrium.

teaching.text: The same system can be pictured **longitudinally**, with the mass moving left and right, or **transversely**, with the mass moving up and down between two springs. Both pictures move in exactly the same way and at the same rate.
children: Both views matter, because one will help with understanding the vocal folds and the other will help with the air in the vocal tract.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate

teaching.text: **When the mass goes up, the frequency goes down, and when the stiffness goes up, the frequency goes up.** A heavier mass is harder to turn around, so it goes back and forth fewer times per second, and a stiffer spring pulls back harder, so it goes back and forth more times per second.
children: So making the mass much heavier lowers the rate of vibration noticeably.
Making the spring much stiffer raises the rate of vibration noticeably.

teaching.text: The two directions of motion keep matching frequencies in every comparison. Whether the mass moves longitudinally or transversely, changing its mass or its stiffness changes the rate in exactly the same way.
children: Once vibration is understood this way, the mass rule feels natural, and the stiffness rule follows from the fact that the stiffer something is, the faster it wants to go back.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes

teaching.text: With two masses, the system can vibrate in **two modes**, and a mode is a way of vibrating defined by whether the masses go together or against each other. When both masses are lifted and let go, they go up and down together, and when one is pulled up and the other down, they go against each other. When both are lifted but one higher than the other, both modes happen at the same time.
**The first mode is slow and the second mode is fast**, even though both use the same masses and the same three springs. The difference is how many springs are actually working in each mode.
children: In the first mode the middle spring never stretches or compresses, so it is not behaving like a spring at all, and effectively the first mode has only two springs.
In the second mode all three springs stretch and compress, so effectively the second mode has three springs.
More springs working means more stiffness, and the stiffer the system is, the faster it has to go back to equilibrium, so the frequency rises.

teaching.text: So **multiple masses give multiple modes, each with its own frequency**. The higher the mode, the more springs are being used, and so the higher its frequency.

sections.title: Three masses have three normal modes

teaching.text: With **three masses** there are three modes. In the first mode all three go back and forth together, the springs hardly stretch, and the frequency is the lowest. In the second mode the middle mass stays frozen while the two outer masses go against each other around it. In the third mode all three go against each other, which has the most stretching and compression and so the highest frequency.

Changing a single part of the system affects each mode differently, depending on what that part is doing in that mode. **Making the middle spring stiffer** affects only the modes that actually stretch it.
children: The first mode stays the same, because its middle spring never stretches or compresses, so its stiffness does not matter.

The second mode rises, because its middle spring is stretched and squished, so a stiffer spring pulls harder. The more stiffness is packed into that one spring, the more the second mode rises while the first never changes.

teaching.text: **Making the middle mass heavier** affects only the modes in which that mass moves.
children: The first mode goes down, because the middle mass moves there and a heavier moving mass slows the system.
The second mode stays the same, because the middle mass is frozen there, and a mass that does not move has no effect on frequency however heavy it gets.
The third mode goes down even more than the first, because the middle mass moves even more in the third mode.

teaching.text: **A mass's influence on frequency depends on how much it moves.** If it does not move at all it has no effect, if it moves a little it has a little effect, and if it moves a lot it has a big effect.
children: These principles are worked out by asking what each part is doing in each mode, not by memorizing a list.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: Adding masses keeps the same patterns, so one mass has one mode, two masses have two, three have three, and so on. Every first mode is the same idea, with everything going up and down together. Every second mode divides the system into two parts, one going up while the other goes down, and when the number of masses is odd, the middle one is frozen. Every third mode divides the system into three parts, with the sides going up while the middle goes down.
children: Lower modes go up and down slowly because they use little stiffness, while higher modes go faster because more springs are stretching and compressing.

teaching.text: Packing in more and more masses and springs gives a **string**, like a guitar or piano string, because a string is an infinite number of masses and springs.
children: Every little piece of a string has weight, which is its mass, and every little piece hates being stretched or compressed, which is its springiness.
In musical instruments, the frequencies of these modes are heard as notes.

teaching.text: A real string vibrates in many modes at the same time, so its motion is the sum of all the modes. Hearing just a single mode would be a very annoying sound called a pure tone, like an ambulance siren, so real sounds always have many modes together.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: The modes of a string fixed at both ends are **harmonics**, which means they are exact multiples of the **base frequency**, the frequency of the lowest mode.

**The multiples come from how many copies of the first mode fit into each higher mode.** The first mode is a single bump that goes up and down, and the second mode fits two of those bumps, one going up while the other goes down, so it vibrates twice as fast.
children: The third mode fits three bumps, so it vibrates three times as fast.
The pattern continues the same way, so each mode's frequency is the base frequency multiplied by how many times the first mode fits into the whole string.

teaching.text: The **spectrum** tells which frequencies a vibration has and how much amplitude is in each one. This string's spectrum has a spike at every harmonic, and because many frequencies happen at once, the actual motion looks erratic, like the waveform of speech.
children: Measured at one marked point, the spikes come out equal, because each mode's strength was set to give the same size there.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: Everything about mass-spring systems can be summed up as a short list of principles, and each one comes from the same two facts, that mass resists being turned around and that springs hate being stretched. **Raising the mass makes the frequency go down, and raising the stiffness makes the frequency go up.** One line of the printed list says that stiffness lowers frequency, but that line is a typo, and the stiffness principle further down the same list agrees that stiffness raises frequency.
children: A system of N masses has N modes of vibration, and each mode has a higher frequency than the one before.

teaching.text: **Increasing a mass lowers frequency in proportion to how much that mass moves, which depends on where it is.** A mass that does not move has no effect however heavy it gets, and a mass that moves a lot lowers the frequency a lot.
children: At the very edges of a string there is no motion, so adding mass there changes nothing.
In the middle of the first, third and fifth modes there is lots of motion, so adding mass there drops the frequency a lot.

teaching.text: **Where there is maximal movement there is no stretching, and where there is maximal stretching there is no movement.** So **increasing a spring's stiffness raises frequency in proportion to how much that spring stretches and compresses**, which also depends on where it is.
children: Where there is no stretching or compression, stiffening the spring has no effect, and where there is lots of stretching, it raises the frequency a lot.

teaching.text: The last two principles are about the ends of the system. When both ends are fixed, the harmonics are whole-number multiples of the base frequency, because the base mode fits a whole number of times into each successive mode. When one end is fixed and the other is free, the frequencies are odd multiples, because the base mode fits an odd number of times into each successive mode.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: Looking again at the string fixed at both ends, the lowest mode has the **most movement in the middle**, where the string just goes up and down without being stretched. The **most stretching is at the sides**, near the fixed ends, where the string barely moves at all.

In higher modes the same thing happens over and over along the string. A stretch with lots of movement and no stretching is followed by a stretch with lots of stretching and no movement, and then by lots of movement again.
children: So where there is the most movement there is the least stretching, and where there is the most stretching there is the least movement.
This alternation does not have to be memorized, since it can be worked out by watching what each piece of the string is doing.

sections.title: A local change affects two modes differently

teaching.text: On a string, one small section is marked where the **fourth mode is moving a lot** while the **fifth mode has no motion at all but lots of stretching**. Raising both the mass and the stiffness of that section has a different effect on each mode, so each effect has to be reasoned out separately.

For the fourth mode, the section is mostly moving. **Raising the mass lowers the frequency**, because the mass is moving there, while raising the stiffness has no effect, because the string there is just moving up and down without stretching.
children: So the frequency of the fourth mode goes down.

teaching.text: For the fifth mode, the section is mostly stretching. **Raising the mass has no effect**, because there is no motion there, while **raising the stiffness raises the frequency**, because there is lots of stretching.
children: So the frequency of the fifth mode goes up.

teaching.text: **Increasing both the stiffness and the mass at that one spot lowers the frequency of the fourth mode and raises the frequency of the fifth.** Where there is no motion, added stiffness raises frequency, and where there is motion, added mass lowers frequency.
children: This method of changing one small part and predicting its effect is called **perturbation**, and it was first worked out on drums by adding wax to different spots.
Wax where the drum vibrated the most made the frequency drop, and wax where there was no motion had no effect.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: **The larynx is a whole membrane**, a surface built from many masses and springs, a bit like a drum. It has many modes of vibration, and they follow the same patterns as before.
children: In the first mode all the masses go up and down together.
In the second mode the left half goes against the right half, and in the third mode the middle is stuck while the sides go against each other.

teaching.text: Just like the string, the membrane's modes are given frequencies that are multiples of the lowest one, and those values are assigned for teaching rather than worked out for that rectangle.
children: Adding all of the motions together gives the combined surface, and its spectrum at one pickup point has equal spikes, one for each mode.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction

teaching.text: **The scientific method depends on very clear theories** about how the world works, usually written as differential equations, and solving the equations gives a prediction of what will be found when the world is actually measured. The theory here is that **the vocal folds are a membrane**, so when they vibrate, their spectrum will have evenly spaced spikes called **harmonics**. The prediction is that **any laryngeal vibration signal will have a spectrum with evenly spaced harmonics**.
The experiment checks this in Praat by taking a spectral slice of a voice. The second spike came out at about double the first, and the third at about triple the first.
children: So the spikes came out evenly spaced, exactly as predicted. Every person's voice has its own base frequency, but the spikes are always multiples of it.

teaching.text: The same reasoning explains how **smoking changes the voice**. Heavy smokers can develop nodules on their vocal folds, and a nodule is like adding a little mass to one spot.
children: Even without a full nodule, smoking changes the stiffness and mass of different parts of the folds.
Those local changes shift different modes by different amounts, just like the wax on the drum, so some harmonics stop being perfect multiples of the base frequency and the voice sounds different.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: A **building** is a system fixed on one side and free on the other. Structural engineers design it to sway in the first mode, all together, and never in higher modes, where some floors would go one way while others go the other way. **The air inside the vocal tract is also fixed on one side and free on the other.**
children: At the bottom, at the vocal folds, the air cannot move, because the folds are closed and the air is stuck there.

At the top, at the lips, the air moves in and out easily. Unlike a building, the air vibrates in all its modes, and changing the masses and springs of different parts of the tract is how listeners know which sound is being made.

teaching.text: A system fixed at one end and free at the other has a different spectrum, because its frequencies jump by **odd multiples** of the base frequency instead of climbing through every multiple. The reason again comes from how many copies of the first mode fit into each higher mode.
children: The first mode goes from no motion at the fixed end to lots of motion at the free end.

The second mode fits three of those pieces, so it is three times the base frequency, and the third mode fits five, so it is five times the base. The pieces always come in odd numbers, because the system must start with no motion and end with lots of motion.

teaching.text: A string fixed at the bottom and free at the top follows the same rule. The fixed bottom is a **node**, a point with no motion, and the free top is an **antinode**, a point of largest motion.
children: For the same length and wave speed, freeing one end halves the lowest frequency.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The air in the vocal tract can be modeled as a **mass-spring chain that is fixed at one end and free at the other**. The masses stand for the air's inertia and the springs stand for its springiness, with the chain fixed at the glottis and free at the lips. The air moves lengthwise, back and forth, so when neighboring bits of air move toward each other the air between them is compressed, and when they move apart it expands.

The first two modes matter most for vowels. The first mode corresponds to **F1**, the lowest air mode of the tube, with its motion still at the glottis and growing toward the lips. The second mode corresponds to **F2**, and it vibrates three times faster than the first.
children: **F1 and F2** are called **formants**, and they are the resonances of the air in the vocal tract.
Three spots are marked along the tube, measured from the glottis, with the spot one third of the way up labeled /a/, the spot two thirds of the way up labeled /i/, and the lip end labeled /u/.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction

teaching.text: Vowels differ in the **shape of the vocal tract**, which MRI images of five vowels make visible. High and low describe tongue height, while front, central and back describe how far forward the tongue is, and together they locate a **constriction**, which is a narrowing of the tract.
children: In Dean the tongue is high and front, which makes a constriction two thirds of the way from the glottis.
In Dune the tongue is high and back, and the vowel has a constriction at the lips.
Done is central with no constriction, Don is low and back with a constriction one third of the way from the glottis, and Dan is low and front with no constriction position marked.

teaching.text: These spots match the marks on the air chain, so each vowel's constriction lands on a different part of each air mode. Where a vowel squeezes the air decides which formants go up and which go down.

sections.title: Blank source page
Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: In the air chain, each marked spot takes part in both modes, but it does not play the same role in both. Near the lips both modes move a lot, while farther inside the tube the second mode has an extra change in its pattern, so a spot can be moving in one mode and compressing in the other.
children: The marks at one third and two thirds of the way up are the spots used to compare the back constriction of /a/ with the front constriction of /i/.
F1 and F2 are resonances of the air in the tract, not harmonics of the vocal folds.

sections.title: /u/ loads the moving lip end

teaching.text: For **/u/**, the masses near the lips get heavier, which is called **loading the free end**. **Motion dominates at the lips in both modes**, because the lip end moves a lot in the first mode and also in the second mode.
children: Added mass where the air moves a lot slows the vibration down.
So for /u/, both F1 and F2 go down.

sections.title: /i/ has opposite effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the constriction is about two thirds of the way from the glottis. In the first mode **the motion of the mass dominates** at that spot, so the added mass wins and F1 goes down. In the second mode **springiness dominates** at that spot, so the added stiffness wins and F2 goes up.
children: This is the same logic as the fourth and fifth modes on the string.
One local change lowers one mode and raises another, because the spot moves in one mode and stretches in the other.

sections.title: /a/ reverses the two effects

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the constriction is about one third of the way from the glottis. In the first mode **springiness dominates** at that spot, so F1 goes up. In the second mode **the motion of the mass dominates** at that spot, so F2 goes down.
children: The result is the reverse of /i/.
The rule never changes, since dominant stiffness raises a formant and dominant mass lowers it, and what changes which effect wins is where the constriction sits.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: Taken together, the principles predict what happens to any mode when a system is changed. To know whether a change raises or lowers a mode's frequency, three things matter, which are what changed, whether mass or stiffness, where it changed, and whether that spot moves or stretches in that mode.
children: Added mass at a moving spot lowers that mode's frequency.
Added stiffness at a stretching spot raises it, and a change at a spot that does neither leaves the mode alone.
The same three questions explain the fourth and fifth modes of the string and the vowels /u/, /i/ and /a/.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: In the uniform tube for **schwa** and in the separate rows for the first, second and third modes, some places have air **moving a lot** and others have air **compressing a lot**, and the two alternate along the tube. **Motion** is how far a bit of air travels back and forth, while **compression** is how much the spacing between neighboring bits of air changes.
children: In the first mode, the air hardly moves near the closed end, where compression is largest, and moves most near the open end.
Higher modes fit more alternating regions into the tube, so strong motion and strong compression trade places along it.
That alternation is why one constriction can push two formants in opposite directions.

sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: The first principle is the simplest one. **As mass goes up, frequency goes down, and as stiffness goes up, frequency goes up.** That principle by itself invites a **false argument**, because if something raises both the mass and the stiffness of a system, it can seem that the two effects cancel and nothing audible changes.
children: That reasoning is only true of a system with a single mass, where more mass and more stiffness really can cancel.
In a system with many masses and springs, the effects do not cancel, because of a fact about where things happen along the system.

teaching.text: **The places with the most motion are the places with the least springiness, and the places with the most springiness have the least motion.** So the location of a change decides which effect counts.
children: At a spot with no movement but lots of stretching, making the spot heavier does nothing, while making it stiffer raises the frequency, so raising both makes the frequency go up.
At a spot with lots of movement but no stretching, making the spot heavier lowers the frequency, while making it stiffer does almost nothing, so raising both makes the frequency go down.

teaching.text: The rest of the principles build on this one, and **they all interact with each other**. A system with N masses has N modes, each with a higher frequency than the last, because more springs are active in the higher modes.
children: Increasing a mass lowers frequency in proportion to how much that mass moves, so a mass that is not moving has no effect at all.
Increasing a spring's stiffness raises frequency in proportion to how much it stretches and compresses, so stiffening a spring in a place with lots of motion has no effect.
When both ends are fixed the harmonics are whole-number multiples of the base frequency, and when one end is free the formants are odd multiples of it.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: Chains with anywhere from one mass up to six masses all follow the same rule, which is that **N masses give N independent modes**. Each chain has fixed ends, equal masses and equal springs, and each row of the grid holds every mode of its chain.

Moving up to higher modes, the pattern has **more reversals and a higher vibration frequency**. In the lowest mode all the masses move together and the springs barely stretch, so the frequency is low. In the highest mode every mass moves against its neighbor, so every spring is working and the frequency is highest.
children: In chains of separate masses like these, the frequencies are generally not whole-number multiples of the lowest one.
Exact multiples belong to the ideal string, which has no separate masses.

sections.title: Why fixed–fixed frequencies are integer multiples

teaching.text: The **vocal folds** are the main system in speech that is fixed on its edges. They sit right behind the Adam's apple and form a membrane of many masses and springs, fixed on all sides, so their vibrations are called **harmonics**. The lowest one is the **base frequency**, and each following harmonic is a multiple of it.
children: So the second harmonic is twice the base, the third is three times the base, and so on.
The base frequency is different for different people, but whatever it is, the harmonics above it are always its multiples.

teaching.text: The multiples come from **counting how many copies of the first mode fit into each higher mode**. On a string fixed at both ends, the first mode is half a wave, with one section going up and down, and that piece from one still point to the next is called a **half-wave packet**.
children: The second mode holds two packets, one going up while the other goes down, so it vibrates at twice the base frequency.
The fifth mode holds five packets, so it vibrates at five times the base frequency.
Higher harmonics fit more half-wave packets into the same length, so each wave is shorter and vibrates faster.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in all of its modes at once. Its combined motion is the sum of all the modes, so the string takes on a changing, complicated shape built from several simple patterns.
children: Higher modes complete more cycles in the same time, so while the first mode swings once, the fifth mode swings five times.
Measured at one point, its spectrum has equal spikes, one for each mode, because each mode's strength was set to give the same size at that point.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: A **membrane** fixed on all of its edges has modes named with two numbers that count its moving regions in each direction. In the (1, 1) mode one region rises and falls as a whole, in the (2, 1) and (1, 2) modes two regions go against each other, in the (2, 2) mode four regions alternate, and in the (3, 1) mode three regions go against each other along one direction.

The same counting works on the membrane. The first mode fits into the second mode twice, so the second vibrates twice as fast, and it fits into the fourth mode four times, so the fourth vibrates four times as fast.
children: The frequencies given to the modes in the picture are assigned for teaching, so they are not the natural frequencies of that rectangle.
The combined surface is the exact sum of all the motions, and its spectrum at one pickup point has equal spikes, one for each mode.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: A **building** is fixed on one side, at the ground, and free on the other, at the top. Engineers want it to sway in the first mode, all together, which is mildly annoying on a high floor but safe. A higher mode, with some floors going one way and others going the other way, would shatter the structure.

A system fixed at one end and free at the other has a **different counting rule**. When both ends are fixed, the basic piece runs from no motion, to lots of motion, and back to no motion, but when one end is free, the basic piece runs only from no motion to lots of motion, with no still point at the free end.
children: The next mode up fits three of those pieces, so it vibrates three times as fast as the first, and the mode after that fits five, so it vibrates five times as fast.
The frequencies of a system fixed at one end and free at the other are called **formants**, and their major property is that they are **odd multiples** of the first.

teaching.text: The string fixed at the bottom and free at the top has a **node** at the fixed end, which is a point with no motion, and an **antinode** at the free end, which is a point of largest motion. So only the odd harmonics occur on this string.
children: For the same length and wave speed, freeing one end halves the lowest frequency.
The big, important system of this kind in speech is the air in the vocal tract, whose vibration makes all the vowels and consonants.

sections.title: Why fixed–free frequencies are odd multiples

teaching.text: The basic piece from a node to an antinode is called a **quarter-wave packet**, and each mode of a system with one free end holds an odd number of them. The first mode holds one packet, the second holds three, the third holds five and the fourth holds seven.

The counts skip the even numbers because of what has to happen at the ends. Adding just one packet would leave a node at the free top, which is not allowed, but adding two packets at a time keeps the antinode at the top.
children: So one fixed end and one free end give only odd multiples, while two fixed ends give every multiple.
In both cases, more packets in the same length means shorter waves and higher frequencies.

sections.title: Count quarter-waves from the boundary conditions

teaching.text: The quarter-wave packets can be counted one mode at a time, from the fixed bottom up to the free top. The first packet appears in every mode, the next two appear from the second mode on, the next two from the third mode on, and the last two only in the fourth mode.
children: That is why the completed counts come out as one, three, five and seven rather than one, two, three and four.
Each pair of packets adds another node and antinode inside the string while keeping the free top as an antinode.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The air in the vocal tract can be modeled as a **chain of masses and springs that is fixed at one end and free at the other**, the same as any other vibrating system. The masses stand for the air's inertia, its tendency to keep moving, and the springs stand for its springiness when squeezed. The chain is fixed at one end, where there is no motion, and completely free at the other.
children: Masses and springs are easier to see than air, but the model and the air itself behave the same way.

teaching.text: The first mode corresponds to **F1**, the lowest air mode of the tube, with its motion still at the fixed end and growing toward the free end. The second mode corresponds to **F2**, and it fits three of the pieces that run from no motion to lots of motion, while the first mode fits only one.
children: So in a uniform tube, the second mode vibrates three times faster than the first.
The letter F stands for formant, so F1 is the first formant and F2 is the second.
Three spots are marked along the tube, with /a/ one third of the way from the fixed end, /i/ two thirds of the way, and /u/ at the free end.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: The air inside the mouth is **fixed at the vocal folds and free at the lips**. At the vocal folds the folds are closed, so the air cannot go back and forth, while at the lips the mouth is open, so the air goes back and forth freely. Air that goes out also comes back in, just as a mass goes back and forth.
children: Each blue circle stands for billions of air molecules.

teaching.text: Two kinds of motion tell the masses and the springs apart. Where neighboring lines of air come really close together and then move really far apart, the air is stretching and compressing, which is a sign of **springiness**. Where the lines of air just move back and forth together without their spacing changing, the air is acting as a **mass**.
children: The easiest place to see pure mass is the free end at the lips, where the air just moves back and forth with no compression at all.

teaching.text: **The first mode of the air is the same idea as a building swaying in its first mode.** There is no motion at the bottom but lots of compression and expansion there, and there is lots of motion at the top but no compression.
children: Higher modes have more fixed points, with one in the first mode, two in the second and three in the third.
Around each point with no motion there is lots of compression, so motion and springiness alternate along the tract.

teaching.text: The formants follow the rule of odd multiples, so the second formant is three times the first and the third formant is five times the first. The actual value of the first formant depends on how heavy and how springy the air is.
children: A recording of schwa, the vowel in hut, came out very close to the one, three and five times pattern that the rule predicts.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction

teaching.text: Vowels differ in **where the air is squeezed** in the vocal tract, and a **constriction** is a place where the tongue or lips narrow the passage and squeeze the air.
children: Done has no constriction, so the airflow is unimpeded everywhere.
Dean is a high front vowel, and it squeezes the air under the roof of the mouth, two thirds of the way from the **glottis**, the tiny space between the vocal folds at the fixed end.

Don is a low back vowel that squeezes the air one third of the way from the glottis, far in the back, while Dune is a high back vowel that also has rounding with the lips very close together, and Dan is low and front.

teaching.text: **The vowel /u/ has two constrictions**, one made with the tongue far in the back and one made at the lips. The constriction at the back has no effect on any of the formants, even though it is large, because of where it falls in the modes.
children: So the lip rounding is the part of /u/ that actually changes the formants.

sections.title: Why a constriction can raise one formant and lower another

teaching.text: **Constricting air makes it stiffer**, just as squeezing the air in a tire makes the tire stiffer. **Constricting air also makes it more massive**, because squeezing air into a smaller volume raises its density, and the smaller the volume, the higher the density.
children: So a constriction raises both the effective mass and the effective stiffness of the air.

teaching.text: The false conclusion is that the two effects cancel, but they do not, since speech is full of changing frequencies even though all a speaker does is raise mass and stiffness in different parts of the tract. The real answer comes from location.
children: At a point with no motion but lots of stretching and compression, the added mass does nothing and the added stiffness raises the frequency.
At a point with lots of motion and no compression, the added mass lowers the frequency and the added stiffness does nothing.
So whether a formant goes up or down depends on whether its mode is moving or compressing at the constriction.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: Watching the air column again with constrictions in mind, each spot along the tube can be asked one question for each mode, which is whether the air there is mostly moving or mostly compressing. **Where the air mostly moves, an added constriction lowers that formant, and where it mostly compresses, an added constriction raises it.**
children: Near the closed end the air is always springy, because air can be squeezed against something closed.
Near the open end the air always acts like a mass, because there is nothing there to squeeze against.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The mass-spring chain makes the same point with masses and springs that can be seen. Near the lips both the first and second modes move a lot, while farther inside the tube the second mode has an extra change in its pattern.
children: So a spot can be moving in one mode and compressing in the other.
The marks at one third and two thirds of the way up are the spots used for the /a/ and /i/ constrictions.

sections.title: /u/ loads the moving lip end

teaching.text: For **/u/**, the masses at the free end get heavier, which is called **loading the free end**. Rounding the lips squeezes the air between them and raises its mass and stiffness. **Both modes are all motion at the free end of the tube**, with hardly any compression or expansion, so the added mass matters and the added stiffness does not.
children: Added mass where there is motion lowers frequency, so both F1 and F2 go down.

teaching.text: **A recording confirms what the reasoning predicts.** Starting from schwa, a student moved into /u/, and both the first and second formants dropped.
children: The increased density of the air between the lips is what lowered them.

sections.title: /i/ has opposite effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the air is squeezed two thirds of the way from the fixed end, and at that spot the two modes are doing different things. In the first mode there is lots of motion and hardly any compression, so the spot is dominated by mass. In the second mode there is lots of compression and expansion, so the spot is dominated by stiffness.
children: So F1 goes down, because added mass where there is motion lowers the frequency.
And F2 goes up, because added stiffness where there is compression raises the frequency.

teaching.text: **A recording confirms this prediction as well.** Starting from schwa and moving into /i/, the first formant dropped a lot and the second formant went up.

sections.title: /a/ reverses the two effects

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the constriction is one third of the way from the glottis, which is closer to the fixed end. In the first mode springiness dominates at that spot, so the added stiffness wins and F1 goes up. In the second mode the motion of the mass dominates at that spot, so the added mass wins and F2 goes down.
children: The result is F1 up and F2 down, which is the reverse of /i/.
The same rule decides both cases, since stiffness where the air compresses raises a formant and mass where the air moves lowers it.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: Across the uniform tube for schwa and the first three modes, motion and compression keep trading places along the tract. **That alternation is what lets one constriction lower one formant and raise another.**
children: A spot that is mostly moving in the first mode can be mostly compressing in the second mode.
So the effect of a constriction has to be worked out separately for each formant.

sections.title: The source supplies harmonics and the filter shapes their heights

teaching.text: In **source-filter theory**, a vowel comes from two systems working at the same time. The **source** is the glottis, the vibrating vocal folds, and **the glottal source gives a harmonic comb**, which is a set of evenly spaced harmonics. Before the vocal tract acts on them, they are just evenly spaced lines of equal height, so nothing in the source marks one vowel from another.
The **filter** is the air in the vocal tract, and **the vocal tract filter sculpts the heights of those harmonics**. For schwa, the filter places its formants evenly up the spectrum.
children: Harmonics near a formant come out tall, and harmonics far from any formant come out short.
So the filtered spectrum rises into peaks around each formant and dips between them.

teaching.text: **The harmonics stay the same and only their heights change, so the outline of those heights identifies the vowel.** That outline, traced by the tops of the harmonics, is called the **envelope**.
children: Changing the vowel does not move the harmonics, because it only reshapes the envelope by moving the formants.

sections.title: The /i/ filter keeps F1 low and F2 high

teaching.text: The same harmonic comb goes through the filter for **/i/**, which has a **low F1** and a **high F2**. The harmonics near the bottom become tall, almost nothing survives in the middle range, and another group of tall harmonics rises up high.
children: Compared with schwa, F1 is lower and F2 is much higher.
That matches the prediction of F1 down and F2 up for a constriction near two thirds of the way from the glottis.

sections.title: The /a/ filter raises F1 and lowers F2

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the filter gives a **higher F1** and a **lower F2**, so the two formants sit close together and the tall harmonics form one broad group fairly low down.
children: Compared with schwa, F1 is higher and F2 is lower, which matches the prediction for a constriction near one third of the way from the glottis.
In both vowels the harmonics stay at the same frequencies, and only their heights change.

sections.title: A spectrogram places successive spectra in time

teaching.text: **A spectrum captures only one instant**, with frequency along one axis and amplitude along the other. But speech is time-varying, since constrictions are made and unmade as the tongue and lips move, so one spectrum is not enough. **A spectrogram stacks many spectra over time.** Time runs along the horizontal axis, frequency runs up the vertical axis, and amplitude is shown as darkness, with high amplitude black, medium gray and low white.
children: So a formant appears as a dark band at its frequency.

teaching.text: In a spectrogram of **/ia/**, the dark bands follow the formants over time. During /i/, F1 is very low and F2 is very high, so there is a dark band low down, a gap, and another dark band high up.
children: Moving into /a/, the formants come close together, as the low band rises and the high band falls.

sections.title: Reflection prompt
Wide harmonic spacing makes formants harder to identify

teaching.text: **Formants can only be seen through the harmonics they shape**, so the spacing of the harmonics matters a great deal. When the harmonics are closely spaced, each formant has lots of harmonics to shape, so each formant band is easy to see. When the harmonics are widely spaced, far fewer of them fall near each formant, and it becomes very hard to tell harmonics from formants.

Holding the filter fixed and changing only **F0**, the base frequency of the vocal folds, a low F0 gives dense harmonics that trace each formant band well, while a higher F0 gives sparser harmonics, so a formant can fall between them. At a very high F0 the formants may look like isolated harmonics instead of bands.
children: So the formants are a smooth envelope and the harmonics are samples of it, and a higher F0 gives fewer samples.
Raising F0 does not move the formants, but it leaves fewer harmonics to reveal them.

teaching.text: High voices make this a real problem for listeners too. A toddler's harmonics are widely spaced, so it is hard to tell where their formants are unless the listener is used to how that toddler speaks.
children: A soprano's first harmonic is very high, so with so few harmonics near the formants, most people cannot follow the words at an opera, even while watching the singer's lips.

sections.title: Homework 4 lab reminder
Speech → Neural Networks
Five membrane modes combine into one motion

teaching.text: Speech has **two major vibrating systems**, and the first is the **vocal folds**, a membrane fixed on all sides and made of a whole bunch of masses and springs. In the first mode all the masses go up and down together, in the second mode half of them go up while the other half go down, and higher modes split the membrane into more and more parts going against each other.
children: This is literally what happens in the throat during speech, and measuring the spectrum of real voices confirms it.

teaching.text: Because the vocal folds are fixed on all sides, their frequencies are **harmonics**, which are whole-number multiples of the lowest one. **The lowest harmonic of all is called F0.** Each person has a different F0, but every voice has its harmonics stacked at multiples of its own F0.
children: The frequencies given to the membrane's modes in the picture are assigned for teaching rather than worked out for the membrane.
Added together, the separate motions make one complicated surface, and its spectrum at a pickup point has equal spikes, one for each mode.

sections.title: A fixed end and a free end select odd harmonics

teaching.text: The second vibrating system is fixed differently, so it follows a different rule, and a **string fixed at the bottom and free at the top** is the simplest version of it. At the fixed bottom the string cannot move, so that point is a **node**, and at the free top it moves the most, so that point is an **antinode**.
children: So every mode must have a node at the bottom and an antinode at the top.

teaching.text: Because of those ends, **only the odd harmonics occur**, at one, three, five and seven times the lowest frequency. With equal excitation of each mode, the spectrum at the free end has equal spikes at those odd multiples.
children: For a string of the same length and wave speed, switching from fixed at both ends to fixed at only one end halves the lowest frequency.

sections.title: Quarter-wavelength packets explain the allowed modes

teaching.text: A **quarter-wave packet** is the piece of a wave that runs from a node to an antinode. That piece is exactly what joins the fixed bottom to the free top, so each mode is built out of these packets. The first mode holds one packet, the second holds three and so vibrates three times as fast, and the third and fourth hold five and seven.
The counts are always odd, because the string must still end with an antinode at the top. Adding one packet would leave a node there, so packets get added two at a time.
children: More packets in the same length means shorter waves and faster vibration.
The packets are pieces of one standing pattern, so they do not travel along the string.

sections.title: Air moves longitudinally in vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: The second vibrating system is the **air in the vocal tract**. Picture the space inside the mouth and throat straightened out into a tube, with the flesh of the tongue, the palate and the throat forming its walls. The air is **fixed at the glottis**, the space between the vocal folds, because the folds are closed and the air cannot move back and forth there, and it is **free at the lips**, where it can go in and out.
children: So the air in the vocal tract is fixed at one end and free at the other, and its frequencies are formants that fall at odd multiples.

teaching.text: The air can be modeled as a mass-spring chain of identical masses in a uniform tube, fixed at one end and free at the other. The first mode corresponds to **F1**, the lowest air mode of the tube, and the second mode corresponds to **F2**, which vibrates three times faster than the first.
children: Three spots are marked, measured from the glottis, with /a/ one third of the way up, /i/ two thirds of the way up, and /u/ at the lip end.

sections.title: Track air motion separately from compression

teaching.text: The air does **two different things** at different places, and both can be seen directly. Where the slivers of air come very close together and then move far apart, the air is compressing and expanding, which is **springiness**, and that happens near the closed end, because air can be squeezed against something closed. Where the slivers stay equally spaced and just move back and forth, the air is acting like a **mass**, and that happens near the open end, because there is nothing there to squeeze against.

In the first mode, the air is very springy at the closed end, then less and less springy and more and more like a mass toward the open end. In higher modes springiness and mass alternate along the tube, and they repeat more times the higher the mode is.
children: In every mode, the air at the open end acts like a mass, going back and forth with hardly any expansion.
And the air near the closed end always acts like a spring.

sections.title: Compare positions within an air mode

teaching.text: Different sections of the vocal tract can be compared by asking, for each one, whether the air there is mostly springy or mostly acting as a mass. A section near the closed end is very springy, a section where the slivers just move back and forth together is acting as a mass, and a section where the slivers bunch up and spread out again is springy.
children: None of this has to be memorized, since it can be read directly from how the air moves.

teaching.text: **Constricting the tract at a springy spot raises the formant of that mode.** A constriction always increases both mass and stiffness, because squeezing air makes it stiffer, the way squeezing a tire does, and bunching it up makes it effectively heavier.
children: At a spot in the third mode where the air is acting like a pure spring, there is no back-and-forth movement, only compression and expansion.
So the added mass does not matter there and only the added stiffness counts, which means the third formant goes up.
This chain of reasoning has to be built fresh at each spot, because the situation is slightly different everywhere.

sections.title: Vowel positions change where the tract is narrowed

teaching.text: Real-time **MRI** images of people speaking reveal where each vowel squeezes the air.
children: In Dean the tongue is high and front, which makes a constriction two thirds of the way from the glottis.
In Dune the tongue is high and back, with a constriction at the lips, and in Done the tongue is central with no constriction at all.
In Don the tongue is low and back, squeezing the air far back in the throat, one third of the way from the glottis, and in Dan the tongue is low and front.

teaching.text: **Combining these images with the model** is where theory meets reality. The model treats the air as masses and springs, fixed on one side and free to move on the other, and a constriction is drawn as stiffer springs and heavier masses at that spot.
children: Where each vowel puts its constriction decides which formants go up and which go down.

sections.title: A constriction changes inertia and restoring stiffness

teaching.text: **Compressing air raises its stiffness**, so constricting at a place with lots of compression raises the frequency. **Bunching up air raises its mass, or density**, so constricting where the air moves a lot adds mass and lowers the frequency.
children: So making a constriction increases both mass and stiffness.

teaching.text: That does not mean the effects cancel and constrictions leave frequency unchanged. **The parts of a vibrating medium that move the most alternate with the parts that compress and uncompress the most**, so at any given spot in a mode, one effect wins.
children: If the air there is mostly moving, the added mass wins and the formant goes down.
If the air there is mostly compressing, the added stiffness wins and the formant goes up.
The same constriction can do opposite things to different formants, because each mode has its own pattern of motion and compression.

sections.title: Use both modes to interpret the same tract location

teaching.text: The same spot along the tract can play different roles in the first and second modes. Near the lips both modes allow strong motion, but farther inside the tube the second mode has an extra change in its pattern, so a spot can be moving in one mode and compressing in the other.
children: That is why the effect of a constriction has to be worked out separately for F1 and for F2.
F1 and F2 are resonances of the air in the tract, not harmonics of the vocal folds.

sections.title: Lip loading lowers both F1 and F2 in the /u/ model

teaching.text: For **/u/**, the lips squeeze the air at the free end, which is called **loading the free end**, and that raises both the mass and the stiffness of the air at the lips. **The air at the open end acts like a mass in every mode**, going back and forth with hardly any squeezing, because there is nothing there to squeeze against.
children: So the added stiffness does not matter, because there is no compression or expansion there.
The added mass does matter, because the air there is moving a lot, so both F1 and F2 go down.

teaching.text: This is what happens in the mouth for the vowels in dune, moon and through. Measurements match it, since starting from schwa, a student's /u/ had an F1 far below the F1 of schwa.

sections.title: A front constriction separates the effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the air is squeezed two thirds of the way from the closed end, and the two modes are doing different things at that spot. In the first mode the air there is mostly moving back and forth, so it acts like a **mass**. In the second mode the air there is mostly compressing, so it acts like a **spring**.

A constriction always raises both mass and stiffness, so the outcome depends on which one matters in each mode. F1 goes down because the air is moving and the added mass wins, while F2 goes up because the air is compressing and the added stiffness wins.
children: So wherever stiffness is what matters, frequency goes up, and wherever mass is what matters, frequency goes down.
Moving from schwa into /i/ in a recording, F1 drops and F2 rises, exactly as predicted.

sections.title: A back constriction reverses the F1 and F2 pattern

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the air is squeezed far back, about one third of the way from the closed end. In the first mode that spot is close to the closed end, and near the closed end there is always springiness, so the added stiffness wins and F1 goes up. In the second mode everything alternates, with compression near the closed end, compression further up, and the motion of the mass in between, right where /a/ squeezes, so the added mass wins and F2 goes down.
children: So /a/ is the opposite of /i/, with F1 up and F2 down.
Students who measured their own /a/ found a high F1 with an F2 not far above it, which fits the prediction.

sections.title: Air motion and compression in the vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: Following one bit of air at a time separates the two features of each air mode. **Motion** is how far a bit of air travels back and forth, while **compression** is how much the spacing between neighboring bits of air changes.
children: A group of air elements can travel far while staying evenly spaced, and elsewhere the elements can barely travel while their spacing changes a lot.
In the schwa tube and in the separate rows for the first three modes, these two features alternate along the length, and that is what decides how each constriction affects each formant.

sections.title: The vocal-fold source sets harmonic spacing

teaching.text: The **vocal folds** differ from person to person, and the rules for mass and stiffness predict their F0. Big, loose, heavy vocal folds have high mass and low stiffness, so their F0 is low and their harmonics are packed closely together. Tighter, lighter vocal folds give a higher F0, and very tight, light vocal folds give an even higher F0, with the harmonics spaced farther apart each time.
children: So a lower F0 packs more harmonics into the same range of frequencies, and a higher F0 spaces them farther apart.

teaching.text: **F0 is not fixed during speech.** Only a robot keeps F0 constant, while real speech changes F0 all the time, in every vowel.
children: The dog slept here, said as a statement, ends with F0 going down, and said as a question, it ends with F0 going up.
Speakers change F0 by changing the stiffness of the vocal folds, and listeners use those changes to understand meaning, and even to tell when someone is sarcastic or pretending.

sections.title: The vocal-tract filter favors nearby harmonics

teaching.text: The air in the vocal tract has its own formants, and for schwa, with no constriction, they sit at the evenly spaced odd multiples that a uniform tube predicts. The exact values vary with how long the vocal tract is and how heavy and stiff the air is. **Formants are all about where the constriction is in the vocal tract.**

The formants interact with the harmonics by one **core rule**, which is that **a formant encourages the closest harmonics to be audible, while harmonics far from that formant are muted.** Harmonics near a formant get amplified, and harmonics farther away get weaker until they cannot be heard.
children: So the shape of the vowel is the filter, the voiced source supplies the harmonics, and the filter chooses which harmonics survive.
Compared with schwa, /u/ has both formants low, /i/ has a very low F1 and a very high F2, and /a/ has its first two formants close together.

sections.title: One filter can look different at different pitches

teaching.text: **The interaction of source and filter is really important.** Picture a person with heavy, loose vocal folds, whose harmonics are closely spaced, saying schwa. There are lots of harmonics near the first formant, so the ones closest to it are amplified and those farther away get weaker, and near the second formant the harmonics are amplified again.
children: So the lower F0 is, the more harmonics the formants have to shape.

teaching.text: Now picture very light, very stiff vocal folds, whose harmonics are widely spaced. The first formant may have no harmonic close by to amplify, so **sparse harmonics can miss a formant or make it look ambiguous**.
children: **Opera singers** have such a high F0 that their formants barely line up with any harmonics, so listeners can hardly hear which vowels they are making.
**Very small children** also have a very high F0, so their formants and harmonics line up so poorly that only their caretakers can easily follow them.

teaching.text: **F0 can be measured in Praat** by taking a spectral slice of a vowel and selecting the lowest harmonic. For a measured male voice, the next harmonic came out at about double the first, so the theory holds.

sections.title: Map spectra into a spectrogram

teaching.text: **A spectrum captures one instant, and a spectrogram stacks many spectra over time.** Time runs along the horizontal axis, frequency runs up the vertical axis, and darkness tells how much energy there is, with high amplitude black, medium gray and low white. So a formant appears as a dark band at its frequency, and its rise and fall over time can be followed.
Speech is not one steady vowel, so the formants are constantly changing. In the spectrogram of /ia/, the lowest band rises from /i/ to /a/, so F1 goes up, and the next band falls, so F2 goes down.
children: These are the same directions as the vowel targets, since /i/ has a low F1 and a high F2 while /a/ has a high F1 and a lower F2.

sections.title: Reflection prompt

teaching.text: A recording of **"Where were you a year ago?"** follows the same rules as single vowels, because real speech is a stream of changing sounds rather than one held vowel. Where F2 rises high, the speaker is making a sound like /i/, since squeezing the air near two thirds of the way up raises F2 and lowers F1.
children: So /i/ is the classic vowel where F1 is low and F2 is high.
In you, all the formants go down, just as /u/ predicts, and across the whole phrase the formants keep going up and down as each sound is made.

sections.title: Speech-complexity experiment prompt

teaching.text: **One experiment reveals how complex listening to speech really is.** A speaker recorded the syllables ma and na, the m sound was cut out of ma, the a vowel was cut out of na, and the two pieces were pasted together. Since the consonant came from ma, the result should sound like ma, but **it sounds like na**.

**Listeners decide which consonant they heard mostly from the vowel that follows it.** In the a that follows m, the formants stay fairly stationary, while in the a that follows n, one formant drops sharply. That drop in a formant inside the vowel tells the listener n, so it overrides the m that was pasted in front.

**Speech perception does not decide sound by sound, slice by slice.** Listeners take in a whole stretch of speech and then decide what they heard, often deciding about a consonant later in time, during the vowel.
children: For decades, speech recognition machines failed because they were built to recognize each little piece separately, the way people think they listen.
An AI that understands speech has to be complex enough to use later information to decide about earlier sounds, and that is why large language models were needed for speech recognition.

sections.title: Use formants as input to vowel recognition

teaching.text: A **neural network** can be trained on formants to decide which vowel is being spoken. The formants from each student's vowels in lab become the network's input, and the **W's**, which are the weights, contain the network's knowledge.
children: Training adjusts the weights until the network makes good decisions about which vowel was produced.
This is where the speech science and the AI come together, since F1 and F2 measured from spectrograms become the numbers the network learns from.

sections.title: A fully connected linear vowel network

teaching.text: This network only multiplies and adds, with **no activation functions** between the layers. It takes two inputs, passes them through three hidden layers, and ends in five outputs, and the two inputs are F1 and F2, the frequencies of the first two modes of the air's vibration.
children: Each hidden layer does **inner products**, multiplying the incoming numbers by its weights and adding them up, and so makes a new representation of the input.
That is like information arriving at the ear and being processed by one part of the brain after another before the brain decides what it heard.
The five outputs are /done/, /dune/, /dean/, /Don/ and /Dan/, with one neuron for each vowel.

sections.title: Random weights assign signed contributions to connections

teaching.text: The example input has a very low F1 and a very high F2, and **a very low F1 with a very high F2 is the pattern for /i/**, so a smart network should decide dean. Before training, every weight is a random number between negative one and one.
children: A positive weight pushes the next neuron up, and a negative weight pushes it down.
The size of a weight sets how strongly its input counts, and these random weights carry no knowledge about vowels yet.

sections.title: Forward flow and an illustrative output distribution

teaching.text: In **forward flow**, the input flows forward through the network one layer at a time.
